extracted_claims.text: Article 43 of the adopted AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) sets out two conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems: internal control (Annex VI) or assessment of quality management system plus technical documentation by a notified body (Annex VII).

For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometric identification), the provider may use internal control or a conformity assessment involving a notified body depending on whether harmonised standards/common specifications have been applied.

Annex VII (notified body) assessment is mandatory for biometric identification systems and certain critical infrastructure AI; most other high-risk AI systems may use the self-assessment (internal control) route under Annex VI.

For high-risk AI systems already covered by existing EU harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I Section A (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow the conformity assessment procedures under that sectoral legislation, with notified bodies also ensuring compliance with AI-specific requirements.

A provider may choose any notified body for the conformity assessment under Annex VII, except that where the high-risk AI system is intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions/bodies/offices/agencies, the relevant market surveillance authority must act as the notified body.
Substantial modifications to a high-risk AI system require a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market.

Article 46 allows a market surveillance authority, by way of derogation from Article 43 and upon duly justified request, to authorise placing on the market or putting into service of specific high-risk AI systems for a limited period for exceptional reasons of public security, protection of life/health, environmental protection, or protection of key industrial/infrastructural assets.

Annex VII section 4.5 provides that a notified body may, as a last resort and upon reasoned request, be granted access to the training and trained models of the AI system, including relevant parameters, subject to existing Union IP and confidentiality law, to assess conformity with Chapter III Section 2 requirements.
Article 35 of the AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) establishes the administrative framework for identification numbers and lists of notified bodies.
As of March 2026, the notified body ecosystem for the AI Act was still being built, with designation processes ongoing across member states and limited capacity.
As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act for medical devices/SaMD intersection with MDR/IVDR.
As of late June 2026, zero notified bodies had been designated under the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) in the NANDO database, a separate but related EU regulatory regime for notified bodies.
As of October 2025, NANDO listed 51 MDR-designated notified bodies and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies, but this pertains to the Medical Devices Regulation/IVDR, not the AI Act specifically.

The Commission has proposed a new Annex XIV for the NANDO information system listing codes and categories corresponding to AI systems subject to Annex I of the AI Act, to support notified body designation under Article 30 of a related regulation.

Post-2026, Notified Bodies designated under the AI Act are expected to begin conducting AI Act-specific conformity assessments, with interplay expected between AI Act and MDR/IVDR notified body assessments for medical device AI.

Under the original 2021 Commission proposal (pre-adoption), Article 43 already set out that for Annex III point 1 (biometric) high-risk AI systems, providers applying harmonised standards or common specifications could choose between listed conformity assessment procedures.

The Commission retains power under Article 43(5) to adopt delegated acts updating Annex VI and Annex VII in light of technical progress, and Article 44 governs certification decisions by notified bodies.

A news blog reports that under a 'final text agreed in September 2026,' the start date for Annex III high-risk AI Act obligations was moved to 2 August 2029 (from a previously reported 2 December 2027), citing lack of readiness of harmonised standards and notified bodies.
Multiple sources state that the high-risk AI Act obligations, including conformity assessment, CE marking and notified body involvement, apply from 2 August 2026.

report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act: Requirements and Notified Body Designation Status

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) establishes two main conformity assessment pathways for high-risk AI systems under Article 43: internal control (Annex VI) and notified body assessment of quality management systems plus technical documentation (Annex VII) (low confidence). While the legal architecture is relatively well-documented, the actual ecosystem of designated notified bodies remains largely unbuilt, and sources disagree on the binding compliance deadline, ranging from 2 August 2026 to a disputed 2029 postponement.

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Routes
Article 43 sets out two primary routes: internal control under Annex VI, or assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body under Annex VII (low confidence) ([PowerQuant](https://powerquant.eu/en/ai-act-conformity-assessment), [Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)). For biometric identification systems under Annex III point 1, providers may choose between internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied (low confidence) ([DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment)). Industry commentary suggests Annex VII assessment is effectively mandatory for biometric identification and certain critical infrastructure systems, with most other high-risk systems eligible for self-assessment (low confidence) ([Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)).

For high-risk AI systems already covered by sectoral EU harmonisation legislation (e.g., medical devices, machinery under Annex I Section A), providers must follow the existing sectoral conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies also verifying compliance with AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)).

### Notified Body Selection and Procedural Rules
Providers may generally select any notified body for Annex VII assessments, except where systems are intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions—in which case the relevant market surveillance authority must act as the notified body (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). Substantial modifications to a high-risk system generally require a new conformity assessment, with an exception for predetermined changes in continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to authorise temporary derogation from standard conformity assessment for exceptional public security, health, environmental, or infrastructure reasons (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Annex VII section 4.5 allows notified bodies, as a last resort, to request access to training and trained models, subject to IP and confidentiality safeguards (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
Evidence on actual designations under the AI Act is thin and largely negative. As of March 2026, the notified body ecosystem was still being built, with designation processes ongoing but limited capacity across member states (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)). As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated at the intersection of the AI Act and MDR/IVDR for medical devices (low confidence) ([AIAct Navigator](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). For comparison, NANDO listed 51 MDR-designated and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies as of October 2025, but these pertain to medical devices regulation, not the AI Act (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). The Commission has proposed a new Annex XIV for the NANDO system to list AI-specific codes/categories to support future designations (medium confidence) ([Council of the EU](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources diverge sharply on the applicable compliance deadline: most sources cite 2 August 2026 for high-risk obligations ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act), [sota.io](https://sota.io/blog/eu-ai-act-eu-declaration-conformity-ce-marking-registration-saas-providers-2026)), while one undated news blog claims a postponement to 2 August 2029 (low confidence, flagged for low reliability) ([news blog](https://ai-act-news-blog.example/annex-iii-deadline-update)). This claim is uncorroborated elsewhere and its legal status (adopted amendment vs. rumor) is unclear. Several low-confidence claims (0.12–0.17) throughout this report—particularly regarding Article 35's administrative framework, delegated act powers under Article 43(5), and the 2029 deadline—warrant caution given weak sourcing.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source confirms specific notified bodies formally designated under the AI Act itself. The legally binding deadline for conformity assessment obligations remains disputed. The procedural relationship between the proposed Annex XIV/NANDO integration and existing Article 43 routes is unclear, as is practical interplay between AI Act, MDR/IVDR, and CRA assessment regimes. No quantitative data exists on notified body capacity or designation timelines across member states.

# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act: Requirements and Notified Body Designation Status

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) establishes two main conformity assessment pathways for high-risk AI systems under Article 43: internal control (Annex VI) and notified body assessment of quality management systems plus technical documentation (Annex VII) (low confidence). While the legal architecture is relatively well-documented, the actual ecosystem of designated notified bodies remains largely unbuilt, and sources disagree on the binding compliance deadline, ranging from 2 August 2026 to a disputed 2029 postponement.

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Routes
Article 43 sets out two primary routes: internal control under Annex VI, or assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body under Annex VII (low confidence) ([PowerQuant](https://powerquant.eu/en/ai-act-conformity-assessment), [Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)). For biometric identification systems under Annex III point 1, providers may choose between internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied (low confidence) ([DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment)). Industry commentary suggests Annex VII assessment is effectively mandatory for biometric identification and certain critical infrastructure systems, with most other high-risk systems eligible for self-assessment (low confidence) ([Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)).

For high-risk AI systems already covered by sectoral EU harmonisation legislation (e.g., medical devices, machinery under Annex I Section A), providers must follow the existing sectoral conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies also verifying compliance with AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)).

### Notified Body Selection and Procedural Rules
Providers may generally select any notified body for Annex VII assessments, except where systems are intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions—in which case the relevant market surveillance authority must act as the notified body (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). Substantial modifications to a high-risk system generally require a new conformity assessment, with an exception for predetermined changes in continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to authorise temporary derogation from standard conformity assessment for exceptional public security, health, environmental, or infrastructure reasons (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Annex VII section 4.5 allows notified bodies, as a last resort, to request access to training and trained models, subject to IP and confidentiality safeguards (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
Evidence on actual designations under the AI Act is thin and largely negative. As of March 2026, the notified body ecosystem was still being built, with designation processes ongoing but limited capacity across member states (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)). As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated at the intersection of the AI Act and MDR/IVDR for medical devices (low confidence) ([AIAct Navigator](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). For comparison, NANDO listed 51 MDR-designated and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies as of October 2025, but these pertain to medical devices regulation, not the AI Act (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). The Commission has proposed a new Annex XIV for the NANDO system to list AI-specific codes/categories to support future designations (medium confidence) ([Council of the EU](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources diverge sharply on the applicable compliance deadline: most sources cite 2 August 2026 for high-risk obligations ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act), [sota.io](https://sota.io/blog/eu-ai-act-eu-declaration-conformity-ce-marking-registration-saas-providers-2026)), while one undated news blog claims a postponement to 2 August 2029 (low confidence, flagged for low reliability) ([news blog](https://ai-act-news-blog.example/annex-iii-deadline-update)). This claim is uncorroborated elsewhere and its legal status (adopted amendment vs. rumor) is unclear. Several low-confidence claims (0.12–0.17) throughout this report—particularly regarding Article 35's administrative framework, delegated act powers under Article 43(5), and the 2029 deadline—warrant caution given weak sourcing.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source confirms specific notified bodies formally designated under the AI Act itself. The legally binding deadline for conformity assessment obligations remains disputed. The procedural relationship between the proposed Annex XIV/NANDO integration and existing Article 43 routes is unclear, as is practical interplay between AI Act, MDR/IVDR, and CRA assessment regimes. No quantitative data exists on notified body capacity or designation timelines across member states.
